Emaciate

ih-MAY-shee-ayt · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To emaciate to become, or to make, abnormally thin, usually from hunger or illness.

Wildlife rescuers said the abandoned horse had been left to emaciate for months before anyone reported the neglect.

Worked Example

Investigators who raided the illegal puppy mill found dozens of dogs so emaciated that veterinarians could count every rib without touching them.

Emaciate describes an extreme, often alarming thinness caused by starvation or disease -- not just being slim.

How Emaciate Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

waste away

waste away: to become progressively thinner and weaker

shrivel

shrivel: to shrink and become thin, especially from lack of food or moisture

Antonyms

fatten

fatten: to make or become fat

nourish

nourish: to sustain with food, promoting health and growth

How Strong Is It? — lean → skeletal → emaciate

lean vs. emaciate

lean vs. emaciate: Lean describes having little body fat in a generally healthy way, much milder than emaciate.

skeletal vs. emaciate

skeletal vs. emaciate: Skeletal describes being reduced to skin and bones, an even more extreme and alarming thinness than emaciate.

Sort It Out

Now place each word on the right side of emaciate.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — e-

prefix — e-: out, thoroughly (intensive) (Latin ex-)

root — maci-

root — maci-: thin, lean (Latin macer, 'thin')

suffix — -ate

suffix — -ate: to make or do; forms a verb (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Latin e- ('thoroughly') plus macer ('thin, lean') plus the verb suffix -ate: literally 'to make thoroughly thin.' Hunger or illness emaciates a body by wasting it away.

Use the root in a new word: meager

Use the root in a new word: meager: The refugees were given only a meager ration of bread and water each day.

Root Check

Word Choice

Emaciate is a strong, often alarming word -- reserve it for extreme, dangerous thinness caused by starvation or serious illness, not just being slim. You'll most often see its adjective form, emaciated.
